Let
\[
E(t)=e^{A_1t}=
\begin{pmatrix}
e^{-\alpha t}&c(t)\\
0&e^{-\beta t}
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where
\[
c(t)=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \kappa\,\frac{e^{-\alpha t}-e^{-\beta t}}{\beta-\alpha},&\alpha\ne\beta,\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \kappa t e^{-\alpha t},&\alpha=\beta.
\end{cases}
\]
Since \(e^{A_2t}=E(t)^T\), the two modes have the same Euclidean operator norm.

For a \(2\times 2\) upper triangular matrix
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\0&b\end{pmatrix},\qquad a,b,c>0,
\]
its largest singular value is
\[
\|M\|_2=\frac12\left(\sqrt{(a+b)^2+c^2}+\sqrt{(a-b)^2+c^2}\right).
\]
Thus define
\[
N(t)=\|E(t)\|_2
=\frac12\left(
\sqrt{(e^{-\alpha t}+e^{-\beta t})^2+c(t)^2}
+
\sqrt{(e^{-\alpha t}-e^{-\beta t})^2+c(t)^2}
\right).
\]

I claim
\[
\Lambda_\tau(\alpha,\beta,\kappa)=\frac1\tau\log N(\tau).
\]

First, this value is attainable. Switch periodically between the two modes, spending exactly \(\tau\) in each mode. Then one two-step block is
\[
E(\tau)^TE(\tau),
\]
whose spectral radius is \(\|E(\tau)\|_2^2=N(\tau)^2\). Hence after \(2n\) dwell intervals,
\[
\|\Phi(2n\tau)\|_2\sim N(\tau)^{2n},
\]
so the exponential rate is
\[
\frac{1}{2\tau}\log N(\tau)^2=\frac1\tau\log N(\tau).
\]

It remains to show no switching law can do better. For any product with dwell lengths \(t_j\ge \tau\),
\[
\|\Phi(t)\|_2\le C\prod_j N(t_j),
\]
where the bounded factor \(C\) only accounts for the final incomplete interval and is irrelevant after division by \(t\).

So it is enough to know that
\[
\frac{\log N(t)}t
\]
is decreasing in \(t>0\). Here is the verification. If \(\alpha=\beta\), then
\[
N(t)=e^{-\alpha t}\left(\frac{\sqrt{4+\kappa^2t^2}+\kappa t}{2}\right)
=e^{-\alpha t}\exp\!\left(\operatorname{arsinh}\frac{\kappa t}{2}\right),
\]
and \(\operatorname{arsinh} x/x\) is decreasing for \(x>0\).

If \(\alpha\ne\beta\), put
\[
m=\min(\alpha,\beta),\qquad \delta=|\alpha-\beta|,\qquad h=\frac{\kappa}{\delta}.
\]
After factoring out \(e^{-mt}\), the remaining norm is
\[
B(x)=\left\|
\begin{pmatrix}
1&h(1-e^{-x})\\
0&e^{-x}
\end{pmatrix}
\right\|_2,\qquad x=\delta t.
\]
With \(u=\tanh(x/2)\) and \(H=\sqrt{1+h^2}\),
\[
B(x)=\frac{\sqrt{1+h^2u^2}+Hu}{1+u}.
\]
Writing \(L(x)=\log B(x)\), direct differentiation gives
\[
L'(x)=\frac{H-\sqrt{1+h^2u^2}}{2\sqrt{1+h^2u^2}},
\]
which decreases from \((H-1)/2\) to \(0\). Hence \(L\) is concave with \(L(0)=0\), so \(L(x)/x\) is decreasing. Therefore \(\log N(t)/t\) is decreasing in all cases.

Thus every dwell interval \(t_j\ge\tau\) satisfies
\[
\log N(t_j)\le \frac{t_j}{\tau}\log N(\tau),
\]
and consequently every switching law has upper Lyapunov rate at most \(\tau^{-1}\log N(\tau)\). The alternating law above attains it.

Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\Lambda_\tau(\alpha,\beta,\kappa)
=
\frac1\tau\log\!\left[
\frac{
\sqrt{(e^{-\alpha\tau}+e^{-\beta\tau})^2+c_\tau^2}
+
\sqrt{(e^{-\alpha\tau}-e^{-\beta\tau})^2+c_\tau^2}
}{2}
\right]
}
\]
where
\[
c_\tau=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \kappa\,\frac{e^{-\alpha\tau}-e^{-\beta\tau}}{\beta-\alpha},&\alpha\ne\beta,\\[6pt]
\displaystyle \kappa\tau e^{-\alpha\tau},&\alpha=\beta.
\end{cases}
\]
